summary: Removes every falsy value from an array and narrows the element type without a cast.
description:
`compact` drops `false`, `null`, `undefined`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""` and `NaN`, and returns what is left in a new
array. The input is not modified.

The point of the function over a plain `array.filter(Boolean)` is the type: TypeScript keeps the original element
type through `filter(Boolean)`, so the caller has to assert the nulls away afterwards. `compact` returns `T[]`
without a cast.

Note that `0` and `""` count as falsy. For values read out of a spreadsheet that is usually the wrong tool — `0` is
a legitimate number and an empty cell arrives as `""` — and `array.filter(nonNil)` removes only the absent values.
returns: a new array holding only the truthy values, in their original order.

examples.title: Dropping the falsy values
examples.body:
```javascript
compact([0, 1, false, 2, "", 3, null]); // => [1, 2, 3]
compact([NaN, undefined]); // => []
compact([0, ""]); // => [] — both are falsy
```

examples.title: Reading a column without the blanks
examples.body:
The column arrives as `Array<string | null>` and leaves as `string[]`, with no cast in between.

<tab title="JavaScript" group-key="js">
<code-block lang="javascript">
function readIds(sheet) {
  const column = sheet.getRange("A2:A").getValues().flat();
  return compact(column);
}

examples.title: When `nonNil` is the better filter
examples.body:
```typescript
import { nonNil } from "apps-script-utils";

const cells = [0, "", 5, null]; // a column read from a sheet

compact(cells); // => [5] — drops the legitimate 0 and the empty cell
cells.filter(nonNil); // => [0, "", 5] — drops only the absent values
```

seeAlso.name: without
seeAlso.note: removes the values you name, rather than the falsy ones.
